metadata.title: Fine Print
metadata.bookend_exempt_reason: Course project film, not a channel episode (INFO 7375 Final Project Film, four parts in the instructor's order, at most five minutes): it opens on the hesitant writer, has no verdict card or Your Turn composer, and no terms card (GATE T failed the fixed-size terms card in October, so terms are defined in the narration). The spoken outro is our own drawn beat with the student's name: the toolkit's ClaudeTitleOutro hard-codes the handle @NikBearBrown, and the course says to narrate as yourself, without the instructor's name, persona or credit line.
metadata.audience: INFO 7375 classmates, TAs and instructor; later, a hiring manager reviewing the project

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Suketh Produtoor. I'm an international student on F-1, looking for new-grad machine learning roles. Before I tailor an application, I need to know one thing: does this posting rule me out?

show.event: backspaces 'company sponsor me' -> 'posting rule me out'

beats.motion_claim: The writer types October's company-level question and corrects it to the posting-level one.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant-writer bookend: the correction is the motion.

beats.narration_text: Titles can't tell me. Earlier this term, a recipe Claude Code and I built screened eight real postings for a fictional new grad, by title and sponsor record. When an AI reviewer read them in full, six asked for two to twelve-plus years of experience, or excluded new graduates.

shot.visual_intent: Eight posting pages in a row, each with a title line and grey text rules (no sponsor ticks: only four of the eight had a sponsor tier); a reading lens passes over them; six get an ink cross over a darkened line, two stay. Labels: '8 real postings', '6 of 8', '2–12+ yrs or no new grads'.

beats.narration_text: So I'm building Fine Print. It will read each new posting, show me the exact sentence behind every requirement that could rule me out, and wait for my approval before anything reaches my shortlist.

beats.narration_text: And postings keep coming. In under two weeks, the three boards I watch showed one hundred seventy-two postings that weren't in my November eighth snapshot. One piece of Fine Print already runs: the watcher. The reader is next.

beats.narration_text: What already exists? My own first try matched on title and sponsor record, and couldn't tell fit. On LinkedIn, I checked two graduate ML postings, from Qualcomm and TikTok. Both separated minimum from preferred qualifications. Neither stated sponsorship.

beats.narration_text: Others have built pieces. Government H-1B data counts an employer's past approvals and denials, not what a posting asks for. Jobscan scores a résumé against a posting and lists missing keywords. One paper flags whether experience and education are required or preferred. And a 2024 study found language models find skills but miss their exact wording.

shot.visual_intent: Four cards, two by two, each showing what that tool gives back, labelled in plain text beside it: 'H-1B approvals · denials · per employer' (USCIS data hub; pairs of bars), 'match score · missing keywords' (Jobscan; a meter and keyword chips, one missing), 'experience, education: required or preferred?' (2025 paper; two blocks), 'skill found · exact wording missed' (2024 study; a check and a cross). No logos.

(2025 paper; two blocks), 'skill found · exact wording missed' (2024 study; a check and a cross). No logos.

beats.narration_text: Fine Print will put those pieces together for one question: should I apply? Each requirement will carry the posting's own sentence, checked word for word by code. Required will stay apart from preferred, silence on sponsorship will mean unknown, and nothing will reach my shortlist until I approve.

shot.visual_intent: The checkpoint scanner checks a sentence slip (a check lands); two trays 'required' and 'preferred'; a grey 'sponsorship: unknown' tag; the approval stamp ('my approval') stays raised over its sheet.

beats.narration_text: Now, how. In October I planned to build the reader first, and now I can build it on top of jobwatch, which already monitors three job boards. Its data: public job-board feeds, read only from an allow-list, each response saved with a fingerprint before anything reads it. The applicant is fictional.

shot.visual_intent: The inspection lamp (the reader, October's plan; drawn faint with a grey 'plan' tag, since it is not built) lands on top of three open crates ('jobwatch', three terracotta lights for the three boards); a permission gate ('allow-list') opens for three feed slips and stops a fourth; the release parcel closes with a terracotta seal ('fingerprint'); a persona card ('fictional applicant').

beats.narration_text: On November twenty-first, Claude Code ran it from a fresh copy. All one hundred sixty-four tests passed. Then a live run read three boards, Anthropic, Databricks and Linear, and found one hundred seventy-two postings it hadn't seen on November eighth.

shot.visual_intent: Two terminal windows replay the saved logs, row by row as they are spoken: the test command, 'Ran 164 tests in 4.180s' and 'OK'; then the run command and the three board lines (jobs=635 new=83, jobs=895 new=88, jobs=32 new=1); '172 not seen on Nov 8' below.

beats.narration_text: Its simple word rule, from my first agent, rejected all one hundred seventy-two for the fictional applicant. Were those rejections right? A word rule can't say. That's the gap the reader will fill.

beats.narration_text: The run also refused to save its memory, because I hadn't approved that: it ended incomplete, state unchanged. On November eighth, I typed that approval myself, for one run and one file, and only then did it save.

Bottom, Nov 8: the command with '--approve-state 2026-11-08-normal-1:state/state.json', 'finished' and 'state advanced: True'.

beats.narration_text: So far, in both job-search agents, I wrote the rules first, before any code. Claude Code wrote the code, all but five of the tests, and ran most checks. I ran my own checks, and twice I withheld my sign-off until the record was right.

beats.narration_text: Next, step by step. By November twenty-fifth, the reader: each claim labelled supported, contradicted or insufficient by the posting's own text, or 'I cannot tell'. By December first, every quote checked against the saved posting. By December thirteenth, my approval tied to the exact shortlist. December twentieth: the full evaluation.

beats.narration_text: Do I have what I need? No API credits: model calls will go through my Claude Code login, as my first agent's judge did for twenty-seven postings in October. Public boards need no accounts; a laptop runs it. The limits: boards can refuse automated reads, and usage caps mean a daily reading budget.

shot.visual_intent: Four stations: a grey 'no API credits' tag and a plug going into its socket ('Claude Code login'); a page stack with a check ('27 judged', 'Oct 31'); the agent workstation ('no accounts', 'laptop'); budget slots with a grey 'plan' tag ('daily budget'), a token lifting and stopping at an ink cap line.

beats.narration_text: How will I know it worked? I'll label real public postings by hand, including a random sample of the ones my rule rejected, and lock a held-out group away before tuning anything.

shot.visual_intent: Three posting pages marked by the kit quill (labelled by hand); two pages pulled from the open 'rejected' crate join them; two go into the 'held out' vault, which locks; the rest go to the 'development' tray.

beats.narration_text: I'll measure four things: whether every quote really appears in the posting; misreads, like 'preferred' read as 'required'; two errors kept apart, clearing the applicant for a requirement they don't meet, and ruling out a posting they'd qualify for; and how often it says 'I cannot tell'.

shot.visual_intent: Four stations on a bench line: the checkpoint scanner with a check ('quote found'); a page with two blocks and a cross ('misreads'); two separate crates ('two errors': 'unsupported clearance', 'false exclusion'); a large '?' ('I cannot tell').
shot.motion_claim: Four stations on a bench line: the checkpoint scanner with a check ('quote found'); a page with two blocks and a cross ('misreads'); two separate crates ('two errors': 'unsupported clearance', 'false exclusion'); a large '?' ('I cannot tell').

beats.narration_text: I'll break it on purpose at least five times: a quote with one word changed, an either-or rule, a posting silent on sponsorship, a board that refuses. And the failure I'm predicting now: a quote copied word for word, but 'five years preferred' treated as a requirement, caught by a separate check.

shot.visual_intent: Five slips in a column ('at least 5'), cracked one by one as each case is named; one slip set apart ('predicted', with ''5 years preferred' → read as required'); the student's own hand label catches it: a label card written by the quill, 'my label: preferred', and an ink cross on the predicted slip. The code quote check is not shown catching it: a true quote passes that check.

beats.narration_text: It worked if at least twenty-seven of thirty held-out decisions match my labels and my checks catch every deliberate failure. It didn't work if the reader misquotes a posting, clears even one unmet requirement, or wrongly rules out more than one eligible posting, regardless of the overall score. I'll label about sixty postings by hand, including thirty randomly picked rejects, and set thirty aside before tuning.

shot.visual_intent: A measuring bar with two zones. 'worked if': '≥ 27 of 30 held-out match my labels' and 'every deliberate failure caught'. 'didn't work if': 'any misquote', 'any unmet requirement cleared', 'more than 1 eligible posting ruled out'. Below: '60 labelled by hand · 30 random rejects · 30 held out'.
